text: Inform, from last lesson, is a phase name. This lesson is what Inform actually looks like on screen: Azure Cost Analysis and AWS Cost Explorer, the two reports you open whenever someone asks why the bill moved. They look nothing alike, but they're answering the same questions with the same basic levers — a date range, a grouping, and a filter.

Azure Cost Analysis lives inside Cost Management and Billing, scoped to a subscription, resource group, or management group. Group By re-slices the same spend by service name, by resource group, by location, or — the one that matters most for allocation — by tag. Granularity switches the chart between daily and monthly buckets, which decides whether you catch a sudden spike or only a slow drift. And there's a forecast line that projects the current month forward from the trend so far — useful for catching a budget overrun early, but it's directional, not a guarantee, and it's slow to react to a workload that only just got deployed.

AWS Cost Explorer is the direct equivalent, and the mental model carries over even though the interface doesn't look the same. Group By covers Service, Linked Account for an AWS Organization with multiple accounts, Region, or Cost Allocation Tag. Filter narrows to one account, one service, or one tag value, the same way Azure's filter panel does. The one AWS-specific wrinkle worth remembering: a Cost Allocation Tag has to be explicitly activated in the Billing console before Cost Explorer will let you group or filter by it — tagging a resource alone isn't enough, which trips up a lot of teams setting this up for the first time.

Here's the pattern you'll use constantly once tagging is in place, with illustrative numbers only: an engineering lead asks whether last month's feature rollout raised the bill. Group by service first — say compute moved from roughly four thousand dollars to fifty-six hundred month over month in this example. Then add a tag filter for that feature's project tag to confirm the increase actually sits inside that team's own resources, rather than somewhere unrelated. Group broadly, then filter narrowly — that two-step read works identically in both tools.

Both tools also carry their own commitment-discount recommendation panels — Reserved Instances and Savings Plans in AWS, Reservations in Azure — previewing the Optimize-phase work Chapter 6 covers in depth. None of that filtering by tag works, though, without a consistent tagging strategy behind it, which is exactly where the next lesson picks up.
